name: Mouth opening / jaw relaxation

lead: This is a no-equipment habit: let the jaw drop and move freely while speaking.
People use it for clearer articulation and a more relaxed face.

paras: Releasing jaw tension lets the mouth open wider and move more easily during speech.
No documented risks; persistent jaw pain is usually something to raise with a clinician.

angle.text: Practitioners say a loose, freely moving jaw makes speech clearer and the face less tight when talking. It is a habit change that needs no equipment.

lead: Mouth opening and jaw relaxation is the practice of letting the lower jaw drop and move freely, without clenching, while speaking or at rest. People use it so that words come out clearer and the face looks softer and less tense, a small change in how they carry and use their face that costs nothing.

Speech clarity is usually described as enunciation or articulation, the ability to speak so each word is heard and understood.[1] Jaw tension and clenching are discussed in dental and physiotherapy literature: Wikipedia describes bruxism as clenching or grinding that can enlarge the masseter, and describes relaxation techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation, yoga and meditation as thought to ease muscle tension.[2][3]

Research that touches the topic is largely about people with jaw disorders: a 2023 meta-analysis of 16 trials with 812 participants found exercise therapy increased active and passive maximum mouth opening in temporomandibular disorders.[4] No published study has tested jaw relaxation as a looks technique in people without such conditions.
infobox: Clinical criteria use pain-free opening of about 35 to 40 mm as a threshold [3]

paras: The practice involves allowing the lower jaw to drop and move without clenching while talking, so vowels and consonants have room to form. It is commonly taught in speech and singing contexts.[1]

Wikipedia's bruxism article describes clenching and grinding as occurring in sleep or awake, with awake bruxism usually semi-voluntary and often linked to stress, and notes that it can enlarge the jaw muscles, particularly the masseter.[2] It also states that relaxation has not been shown to reduce bruxism symptoms though it may improve well-being, and that biofeedback has limited evidence.[2]

The article on temporomandibular joint dysfunction describes limited jaw movement as one of three classic signs, lists relaxation techniques and gentle stretching within pain tolerance as home methods, and uses measured pain-free opening of 35 to 40 mm or less in diagnostic criteria.[3]

No studies found of jaw relaxation for facial appearance or speech presentation. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (812 participants) in temporomandibular disorders found exercise therapy associated with less pain and larger active and passive maximum mouth opening.[4] A 2023 review of the joint's biomechanics describes how disc displacement alters jaw movement.[5]
Community members describe it as a free adjustment to how they speak and carry their face, usually grouped with posture and facial-expression habits.
